item.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
item.abstract: This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings. Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms. But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis. Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover different positional methods in LLMs; what methods are used by recent open LLMs. Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) . If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher: The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style. PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses. PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures . Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here , which also has a navigation bar on the left side. Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token. The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation. A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention. We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed. Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example: “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.” “The gray fox jumps over the red fox.” Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure. For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7. (If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my tokenizer materials on GitHub .) Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer. Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair. GPT-style models do use a causal (autoregressive) mask, which restricts each token to itself and earlier tokens. Interestingly, this causal mask gives the computation some implicit order information. In our example, “jumps” can attend to “red” in the first sentence and “gray” in the second. So, a causal LLM can theoretically already distinguish these sentences even without explicit positional embeddings. (We will return to this idea later when discussing the “NoPE” concept.) Nonetheless, GPT-2 and most newer LLMs include explicit positional information because it gives attention a direct signal about positions. That’s because even though the causal mask determines which tokens are accessible and provides implicit order information, it doesn’t distinguish a separation of one position from a separation of ten, for example. So, explicit positional methods are still useful (or even essential), since they supply that information. If this all sounded confusing, don’t worry, it was more meant as an overview, and we will step through these concepts a bit more slowly in the remaining article. We briefly talked about implicit positional information through causal attention masks (and we will revisit this again in more detail later). However, we now switch gears and talk about the explicit ways to add positional information. The perhaps simplest and most direct (but not “cheapest”) approach is to give each sequence position its own vector. We add that vector to the token embedding, so the resulting, modified embedding vector is then passed to the first transformer block. This exact procedure is discussed in the following subsections. To illustrate the use of an explicit, learned positional vector to the input embeddings, let’s consider GPT-2 as a concrete example. GPT-2 learns a table of position vectors during training. The following figure illustrates where these vectors are used in the architecture, that is, immediately after the token embedding lookup and before the first transformer block. The positional embedding layer depicted in the figure above follows the same implementation as the token embedding layer, i.e., they have exactly the same output dimensions so that the resulting input vectors can be added to each other. The code below shows that with an excerpt of a GPT-2 code implementation: And in mathematical terms, we can write it as follows. Let m be a position index and x m the token ID at that position. The input to the first block is E token is the embedding layer, P m is the position info vector selected by m , and h m is the resulting summed embedding and position vector. The two vectors have the same width, so we add their entries element-wise.

item.title: Bland Launches Tofu-1, a Full-Duplex Speech-to-Speech Model for Calls
item.abstract: Bland, the San Francisco voice-AI company, has released Tofu-1 , a full-duplex speech-to-speech model in research preview. The Tofu-1 speech-to-speech model targets calls from moving cars, hospital rooms and weak-signal lines. It listens while it speaks and reasons while it talks. For phone-agent teams, one model now handles audio in and audio out, with no transcript between. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Tofu-1 is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model from Bland that hears, reasons and replies in audio during phone calls. It is the first release in a planned family of Bland speech-to-speech models. Most voice agents are cascades. They turn speech into text, pass it to a language model, then turn the reply back into speech. Tofu-1 listens to the audio directly , so tone, hesitation and background sound stay available to the model. Bland has not published the internal architecture. Bland lists 3 audio skills on its product page: Callers can interrupt or correct Tofu-1 mid-sentence. While it works on a request, it keeps the conversation moving. It reports the result only when the work is done. It never claims a task is finished early. Because Tofu-1 models the sound of a call, it can also produce one. That includes a second speaker, the room around them and line noise. The TV Test asks one question: can the model follow the caller while ignoring speech from another scene? TV audio is often louder than the caller. Bland marks its TV Test walkthrough as illustrative, not recorded model output. Competitor figures come from each vendor’s own page. FDB results use different benchmark versions and are not directly comparable. Research preview access is open to a limited number of enterprises. Bland names banking, healthcare, insurance and government as target sectors. The sign-up form asks for monthly call volume, from under 1,000 to 50,000+. Check out the Tofu-1 product page , the launch post on X and the research preview sign-up . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Need to partner with us for promoting your GitHub Repo OR Hugging Face Page OR Product Release OR Webinar etc.? item.title: 🗞️Nvidia Without Jensen, Alibaba’s Chip IPO, and Qwen4’s First Look
item.abstract: China AI Weekly Digest summarizes the week’s big news, model updates, compute, policy, products, and research, drawn from the China AI Index newsfeed . The digest is (mostly) compiled and drafted by an AI agent using credible news outlets; I fact-check and edit it. Read to the end for “One to Watch” as this week’s video pick. This week: 248 stories tracked (0 editor picks, 99 English-language, 149 Chinese-language 🇨🇳) over 2026-11-07–2026-11-14. Alibaba discloses a Hong Kong listing application for its chip unit. Alibaba said on November 10 that T-Head had confidentially filed for a Hong Kong listing on September 11. T-Head designs chips for data-center workloads, making it part of Alibaba’s own effort to build out AI infrastructure. A listing would give investors a separate way to value that chip business while keeping it within the group, as Alibaba expects T-Head to remain a subsidiary. Final offering terms, including how much the unit might raise, are still pending. ( SCMP / 雷峰網 / HKEX ) MiniMax and ByteDance give image generation a production workflow. MiniMax released H3 Image with open weights and made it available through its API, MiniMax Code and Hailuo. The model generates images at native 4K and accepts up to 16 references, giving users more control over which elements carry into the result. ByteDance began rolling Seedream 5.5 into Doubao, Doubao Work and Jimeng, with localized edits and support for generating images with transparent backgrounds. ( 量子位 / 雷峰網 / @MiniMax_AI / @BytePlusGlobal ) Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia faces renewed scrutiny over chip exports and mounting U.S.–China tensions. Nvidia said Huang stepped down as CEO and from its board effective November 11, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO. The board has launched an independent investigation into allegations surrounding Huang and Nvidia’s China business. Huang’s departure could reshape the global AI landscape, particularly U.S.–China technology competition. A vocal opponent of restricting chip sales to China, Huang had argued that keeping Chinese developers within Nvidia’s ecosystem served American interests. His exit comes as bipartisan lawmakers push for tighter export controls, including potential restrictions on overseas cloud access to advanced AI chips. ( Nvidia 8-K / Reuters ) This week brought downloadable weights from Meituan, a new speech model from Tencent and previews from Baidu and Qwen. Meituan published the LongCat-2.5 weights under the MIT license, giving developers a way to run or adapt the multimodal model themselves. Meituan lists 1.6 trillion total parameters and about 48 billion active per token, with the model built for tasks that combine visual understanding and agentic coding. ( VentureBeat ) Baidu introduced ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview, a separate release from ERNIE 5.5 Base. Its demonstrations focused on practical tasks, including generating interactive 3D scenes through code and handling knowledge-work assignments. ( 雷峰網 ) Tencent released Hy Realtime, a Hunyuan speech model for live voice interaction. The model takes speech input and generates spoken responses, giving developers a model designed for conversational audio. ( 第一財經 / IT之家 ) Alibaba previewed Qwen4-Max, the first model in its next-generation Qwen4 family, on November 11. The multimodal model supports text, image and video inputs, a 1 million-token context window, and reasoning capabilities designed for coding, complex agentic tasks and knowledge work. ( @Alibaba_Qwen ) BytePlus announced Seedance 2.5 Flash and quoted US$0.152 per second for 720p text-to-video and image-to-video. It says Flash is nearly twice as fast as the flagship. ( @BytePlusGlobal ) Server makers moved toward public markets while policymakers looked at who can buy advanced chips and where those chips end up. Chinese AI server maker xFusion cleared a Shenzhen Stock Exchange review for its proposed ChiNext listing, Reuters reported. The planned offering is sized at about US$1.2 billion, and the review clears one stage of the listing process. ( Reuters ) SMIC expects tight AI computing supply to persist until 2028, according to SCMP. The foundry’s forecast puts a timeframe on the capacity pressure facing AI developers as Washington weighs tighter controls on advanced chips. ( SCMP ) Malaysia is considering closer oversight of data centers to curb the resale and diversion of advanced AI chips, Caixin reported. The proposal would bring data-center operators into the enforcement picture by focusing on what happens to chips after they enter the country. ( 財新 ) U.S. Senator Tom Cotton urged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to block Chinese DRAM maker CXMT from the U.S. market. The request targets access to U.S. buyers and would require action by the administration. ( Reuters / CNBC ) Kimi’s maker took preparatory steps toward a listing, while two robotics rounds funded manufacturing and factory deployments. Moonshot AI is restructuring ahead of a potential IPO, the WSJ reported. The Kimi developer is moving shareholder interests from a Cayman Islands structure into a Chinese entity. The Journal put its latest private valuation at US$50 billion. ( WSJ ) UniX AI closed a RMB500 million pre-A round, with Greenland Group joining as a strategic investor. The Suzhou robotics company says the money will help it scale production and deliveries of its general-purpose humanoids. ( 投資界 / 新京報貝殼財經 ) Zhifeng Chuangyuan raised RMB80 million in an angel round. The company has introduced its wheeled, dual-arm Z100 and plans to spend the money on R&D and expansion into optical-module manufacturing, where robots need to perform precise insertion and removal tasks. ( 投資界 ) Beijing set a robot manufacturing target, Shanghai laid out rules for scientific data, and U.S.–China safety talks surfaced a basic question about incident reporting. Beijing’s 2026–2028 embodied robotics plan calls for local production capacity of 200,000 finished robots a year. The city will support both contract manufacturing and companies’ own production lines, alongside shared facilities across Beijing, Tianjin and Hebei to speed up parts prototyping. ( 財聯社 / 北京市政府 ) Shanghai issued trial rules on preserving, classifying and sharing scientific data. The measures also encourage research institutions and AI developers to work together, putting scientific datasets within reach of more model-development projects where sharing is permitted. ( 第一財經 / 上海市科委 ) Washington and Beijing established a channel to discuss risks from advanced AI. Analysts told SCMP that agreeing on what counts as a “serious” incident could be an early hurdle. That definition would shape which events either government is expected to bring to the other’s attention. ( SCMP ) DeepSeek opened up tools from its consumer app, while Qwen added an agent that colleagues can use together. DeepSeek opened APIs for capabilities already used in its app, including search, document and link ingestion, voice and safety checks. Developers can also call standalone services for optical character recognition, speech recognition and speech synthesis. ( 第一財經 / @deepseek_ai ) Qwen Office 2.0 introduced Team Agent, a shared workspace where colleagues can work with the same assistant. A group can bring its own materials into a shared task and collaborate on the output in that workspace. ( 量子位 / 雷峰網 ) Apple completed Chinese generative-AI service filings covering tablets and laptops. The filings extend the registered device categories for Apple Intelligence. The report gave no rollout date for either category. ( 第一財經 ) Robot teams tested how touch and movement transfer across hardware and environments, while a new drug-discovery model took on biomolecular benchmarks. Ant-backed Robbyant’s LingBot-Touch learns a common representation across pressure-sensitive, magnetic and camera-based tactile sensors.

item.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
item.abstract:
This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why. First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering. The second reason is legal: purely AI -generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute , which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI . Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI -generated images to be tagged as Public Domain . However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI -generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license. Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source. If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: @jcubic and on LinkedIn .

item.title: Nvidia deliberately kept GPU prices high through circular financing deals
item.abstract:
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years. TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust . Connecting the dots: The AI boom has been widely blamed for GPU prices spinning out of control over the past year. Following Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia,new information suggests that this was the goal of the former CEO's business strategy, which has long drawn accusations of circular financing. A recent Wall Street Journal profile of Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress has shed more light on how Nvidia controversially financed its own customers to drive the AI boom. According to the report, the company pushed for more deals in mid-to-late 2026 to absorb an oversupply of TSMC wafers and keep GPU prices high. Since at least last year, Nvidia has been accused of prolonging the AI boom by supporting the companies that buy its chips. Co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, along with CFO Kress, even went so far as to defend the company against comparisons to Enron, which used similar tactics to illegally obscure its debt before its 2001 collapse. Also read: GPU Prices Are Spiraling Out of Control - Q4 2026 Update Behind the scenes, Kress expressed concern about the scale of the deals Nvidia had inked with cloud providers and major AI companies like OpenAI. Nvidia pushed ahead anyway, but by summer 2026, the company was wondering whether it had pushed too far amid an "avalanche" of semiconductors it had ordered from TSMC. It was around this time that Huang berated Kress, calling her "a deer in headlights," according to someone familiar with the matter. Nvidia began to slow down, downsize, and pause some of its financing deals, including one with OpenAI that originally included a $250 billion backstop for the world's largest data center. Source: Bloomberg AI data centers have siphoned off DRAM and NAND manufacturing capacity traditionally used for RAM and storage in consumer devices, inflating prices. Nvidia's GeForce GPUs have been hit especially hard, with prices often exceeding 160% of their original MSRP. The company's flagship RTX 5090 has become unobtainable because Nvidia has directed its VRAM and semiconductors toward data center GPUs. As its financial support deals wound down, Huang became worried about the company's stock market valuation, with its average monthly stock multiple falling far behind those of other large tech companies. Related: Without Jensen Huang, is it game over for GeForce? Colette Kress, Interim CEO and Executive VP and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) of Nvidia. At a Berlin conference, the former CEO told major clients a story about a busy Japanese soup vendor who refused to give him a second serving after he had waited in a long line, saying the vendor had too many customers and not enough soup. Huang used the story to highlight the value of maintaining a diverse customer base and keeping prices high, suggesting that Nvidia's circular financing strategy inflated GPU prices by creating the perception of high demand. The story emerged after Huang's resignation following the revelation of multiple extramarital affairs. One was with Alice Huang (no relation), whose company, Megaspeed, was suspected by US intelligence of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of export regulations. While some allege that she is a spy for Beijing, President Trump and the Justice Department said that hasn't been determined. 49 comments 5.2K likes and shares See more TechSpot in Google Add us as a preferred source and our reporting shows up first when you search. item.title: US IRS free online tax filing open source repo (2025)
item.abstract:
Direct File Direct File is a service from the United States Government that provides taxpayers the option to electronically file their federal tax return for free, directly with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Direct File is an interview-based service that is intended to work as well on a mobile phone as it does on a laptop, tablet, or desktop computer. It is available in English and Spanish and is designed to be accessible to taxpayers who have a variety of attitudes, aptitudes, abilities, and access needs. Direct File interprets the United States' Internal Revenue Code (26 USC) as plain language questions, the answers to which should be known to taxpayers without need of external instructions or publications. Taxpayers' answers are then translated into standard tax forms and transmitted to the IRS's Modernized e-File (MeF) API, which is available for authorized public use. These questions and logic, developed in close collaboration with the IRS Office of Chief Counsel , as well as the associated test cases and scenarios, may be useful for others working on products that need to accurately interpret United States tax law as of Tax Year 2024. Direct File also incorporates the Fact Graph, a declarative, XML-based knowledge graph data structure that is designed to reason about incomplete information, such as a partially completed tax return. The Fact Graph is written in the Scala programming language; it runs on the JVM on the backend and is transpiled via Scala.js to run on the client as well. Direct File's Fact Graph is not domain-specific, and it may be useful to revenue agencies and as a reference for business rules engine implementations. Although Direct File only files federal tax returns, United States taxpayers also have state and local filing obligations. Direct File facilitates the completion of these obligations by enabling taxpayers to optionally import their federal return data into a third-party tool that can file state and/or local taxes, without needing to reenter information. This transaction is enabled via a State API, which transfers both standard MeF XML as well as an enriched JSON format that includes additional data elements that were identified as being useful to state revenue agencies to streamline the state tax experience. Direct File was developed by an in-house team of technologists at the IRS. The blended, cross-agency team included support from USDS and GSA , as well as vendor teams TrussWorks , Coforma , and ATI . For a more details on the program and its history see https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p5969.pdf and https://www.irs.gov/filing/irs-direct-file-for-free This repository has been archived and is no longer maintained. The code is provided for historical reference and may contain unpatched or unknown vulnerabilities. It should not be used in production systems. Where do I start? See ONBOARDING.md if you want to jump into running Direct File locally Exempted Code Not all source code, documentation and metadata used in the development of Direct File is included in this repository. Specifically, any code or data that is considered Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Federal Tax Information (FTI),
Sensitive But Unclassified (SBU), or source code developed for National Security Systems (NSS), as defined in 40 U.S.C. § 11103, is exempt. Due to these restrictions, certain pieces of functionality have been removed or rewritten. Authorities Legal foundations for work include: Source code Harmonization And Reuse in Information Technology Act" of 2024, Public Law 118 - 187 OMB Memorandum M-16-21, “Federal Source Code Policy: Achieving Efficiency,
Transparency, and Innovation through Reusable and Open Source Software,” August 8,
2016 Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Part 27 – Patents, Data, and Copyrights Digital Government Strategy: “Digital Government: Building a 21st Century Platform to
Better Serve the American People,” May 23, 2012 Federal Information Technology Acquisition Reform Act (FITARA), December 2014

item.title: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft
item.abstract: While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once. In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang. Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry ; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league. In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.” Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night. “Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday . When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.” “Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”
